newsitem.title: GERMANY: German upper house votes through 1997 tax bill.
newsitem.headline: German upper house votes through 1997 tax bill.

text.p: Germany's Bundesrat upper house of parliament on Thursday passed Finance Minister Theo Waigel's 1997 tax bill into law, in a vote which was a formality after government and opposition worked out a hard-fought compromise.
The measure had been held up by the Bundesrat, controlled by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), over government plans to abolish wealth taxes next year.

But the SPD caved in, unable to resist a court ruling that the tax was illegal, and eventually agreed in parliament's mediation process with the coalition government on tax hikes to offset the resulting loss of revenue.
The demise of wealth taxes will strip 9.3 billion marks in revenue from Germany's 16 states, while increases in property trading taxes and inheritance taxes will raise 8.1 billion.

Passage of the tax bill wraps up legislation on state finances for 1997, when Waigel wants to bring the public sector deficit down to 2.5 percent of gross domestic product, thereby qualifying for planned European monetary union in 1999.
Separately, government leaders were expected at 1100 GMT to announce key tax cuts to take effect in 1998 agreed at coalition talks on Wednesday.
The solidarity surcharge, raised to channel aid to eastern Germany, will fall by two points from 7.5 percent, while cuts in corporation tax are also planned, coalition sources said.
